leads_only: Counts of catalogued identities and a population estimate. Nothing here admits an order, authenticates an identity, assigns a status, or changes a numbered-series count.
unnumbered_series_observed_note: Lower-bound census: identities found by Lord 1943 (all years, 1789-1941) or by the completeness cluster list (1789-1899), after deduplication by the rule below.
estimate_sensitivity_note: The estimate depends strongly on the matching threshold (see capture_recapture.sensitivity_to_matching_threshold); the interval covers sampling error at the chosen threshold only.
unnumbered_series_estimate_95_note: Chapman interval for the day-precise 1789-1899 pool, plus every other observed identity taken as observed only (month- or year-precise dates, and Lord rows 1900-1941): a floor, since no unseen count is estimated for those.

dedup_rule.text: A Lord row and a cluster mention are one identity when both dates are day-precise and equal and the subjects share at least two distinctive words (5+ letters, not on census-completeness's stop list). See unnumbered.py.

capture_recapture.years_covered_by_both_lists: 1789-1899 (the cluster list reads no source after 1899; Lord runs to 1941, so Lord rows 1900-1941 are outside the overlap)
capture_recapture.list_1: identities with at least one Lord 1943 row, day-precise date
capture_recapture.list_2: identities with at least one mention from another project source (Richardson, GPO 1912, MR and GLO books), day-precise date
capture_recapture.estimator: Chapman N=(n1+1)(n2+1)/(m+1)-1; Seber variance (n1+1)(n2+1)(n1-m)(n2-m)/((m+1)^2(m+2)); 95% interval S+f0/C..S+f0*C, S=n1+n2-m, f0=N-S, C=exp(1.96*sqrt(ln(1+var/f0^2)))

assumptions.may_fail_because: The target is orders signed 1789-1899 and absent from no printed list; the cluster list is built from later printings (1880-1916), so orders revoked or never printed are in neither list; a Lord entry can describe a signed order or only a departmental act (Richardson prints both). Direction: unclear; a loose boundary inflates the Lord-only count and so the estimate.

Lord (1943) cites the General Land Office, War Department, Indian-reservation and Richardson volumes as his sources, so an order in those books is more likely in Lord. Positive dependence makes m too large, so N is UNDER-stated: the interval is a floor on the true uncertainty, not a ceiling.

Large, well-known orders (big reservations, named parks) are caught by every list; small or unusual ones by none. Heterogeneity again under-states N. Day-precise dates are caught more often than year-only ones, so the estimate is restricted to day-precise identities and says nothing directly about the rest.

The rule needs an exact day-precise date and two shared distinctive words; OCR errors in dates or subjects make true matches fail (m too small, N over-stated); same-day orders about similar places can merge falsely (m too large, N under-stated).

capture_recapture.direction_of_bias: Dependence between Lord and the printed sources and unequal catchability both under-state the total; OCR failures to match over-state it. Read the interval as a floor on uncertainty.
